You will learn why these calls cost no gas, how to create a JavaScript contract instance using an ABI and address, and how to call view and pure functions with. call(). We also cover event queries. Smart contracts emit events to log important actions. You will see how to use getPastEvents to retrieve those logs, read their returnValues, and filter by block ranges or indexed fields. By the end, you will understand the difference between. call() and. send(), how public variables produce automatic getters, and common mistakes to avoid like using the wrong ABI or an incorrect address. Think about a UI that needs a token balance or a registry lookup — read operations are the efficient, correct tool for that job. Ready to explore contract instantiation, data reads, and historical logs? Let’s begin.

screens.title: What are Read Operations? (view & pure)
screens.narratorSegment: Read operations are contract calls that do not alter blockchain state. In Solidity these appear as view or pure functions. A view function may read state variables but does not modify them. A pure function does not even read state; it only computes a result using its inputs. Both categories can be executed locally by your connected node, so they do not create transactions and do not consume gas. Why this matters: user interfaces frequently need current values such as balances, ownership, or computed results. Using. call() for view and pure functions makes these queries fast and free. For example, a dApp that displays a token balance calls balanceOf(address). call() to get the value immediately. A pure function that computes a price ratio from input numbers can be called to preview a calculation without writing to the ledger. A common misconception is to think. call() will change state. It will not. If you need to change state you must send a transaction with. send(). Another pitfall is assuming view calls always read the chain exactly the same across nodes; the node's state and syncing status matter. For quick UIs and analytics, view and pure calls are the correct, efficient tool. Key takeaway: use. call() for reads, and reserve. send() for actions that must change the blockchain.

keyIdea.title: Read operations summary
keyIdea.text: View and pure functions run locally via .call(), are gas-free, and are ideal for UIs and read-only computation.

content.html:
Core Concept › Read Operations
Definition and Cost Model
View reads state, pure computes without state. Both are executed locally and cost no gas.
When to use .call()
  • Fetch balances, owner addresses, or stored values.
  • Preview calculations performed by pure functions.
  • Populate UI elements without prompting a transaction.
Misconceptions
  • .call() will not persist state changes. Use .send() for transactions.
  • A wrong ABI or address will cause function-not-found errors.
  • Node sync state can affect read results on non-finalized chains.
Concrete Examples
Example: Read a stored value
Contract method getData().call() returns a number without a transaction.
Example: ERC-20 balance
Call balanceOf(address).call() and convert from token units with fromWei to show user balance.
Key Takeaway
Reads are fast and free. Use them for UIs and queries. Reserve transactions for state updates.

screens.title: Instantiate web3.eth.Contract
screens.narratorSegment: Instantiating a contract in Web3. js is the first practical step for read operations. You need two things: the contract ABI and its deployed address. The ABI is a JSON description of public functions and events. The address tells the node which on-chain bytecode to interact with. With those, create an instance using new web3. eth. Contract(abi, address). That instance exposes a methods object and event helpers. A simple process: 1) Acquire the ABI from the compiled contract artifact. 2) Confirm the deployed address from your deployment tool or Ganache console. 3) In your script, initialize Web3 with a provider and then create the contract instance. 4) Use contract. methods. name(). call() or contract. methods. variable(). call() to fetch data. 5) Use contract. getPastEvents(...) to fetch logs. Concrete example: using the SimpleStorage ABI and a Ganache address, the script creates const simpleStorage = new web3. eth. Contract(simpleStorageABI, simpleStorageAddress). You can then await simpleStorage. methods. getData(). call() to read a number. Watch out for the common mistake of leaving a placeholder address in the code. That will cause errors or null results. Keep ABI and address management consistent between your build and runtime environments to avoid mismatch errors.

keyIdea.title: Instantiation steps
keyIdea.text: Gather ABI and address, create new web3.eth.Contract(abi, address), then call methods or getPastEvents on the instance.

content.html:
Process Flow › Instantiate Contract
Step-by-step
  1. Obtain ABI from your compiled artifact.
  2. Get deployed contract address from deployment logs or Ganache.
  3. Create a Web3 provider, then new web3.eth.Contract(abi, address).
  4. Call view functions with .call() or query events with getPastEvents.
Quick note
ABI must match the deployed bytecode. An ABI mismatch leads to function-not-found errors.
Code snippet
const Web3 = require('web3');
const web3 = new Web3('http://127.0.0.1:7545');

const simpleStorageABI = [ /* ABI JSON */ ];
const simpleStorageAddress = '0x...';

const simpleStorage = new web3.eth.Contract(simpleStorageABI, simpleStorageAddress);
const value = await simpleStorage.methods.getData().call();
console.log('Value:', value);
Example output: Value: 100

screens.narratorSegment: In this demo we walk through the SimpleStorage read script. The contract exposes a public data variable and a getData view function. keyIdea.text: Use .call() to read getData() and owner(), and never expect .call() to persist state changes.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough › SimpleStorage Read
Starter script (visual)
const Web3 = require('web3');
const web3 = new Web3('http://127.0.0.1:7545');

const simpleStorageABI = [ /* ABI for SimpleStorage */ ];
const simpleStorageAddress = '0x...';

async function readContractData() {
  if (simpleStorageAddress === '0x...') {
    console.error('ERROR: Please deploy and update the address.');
    return;
  }

  const simpleStorage = new web3.eth.Contract(simpleStorageABI, simpleStorageAddress);
  const currentData = await simpleStorage.methods.getData().call();
  const contractOwner = await simpleStorage.methods.owner().call();
  console.log('Current stored data:', currentData);
  console.log('Contract Owner:', contractOwner);
}

readContractData();
Expected console output (example)
--- Interacting with Smart Contract (Read) ---
Current stored data: 100 Contract Owner: 0x1234...abcd
Common mistake
Leaving the placeholder address causes the script to exit or throw. Always confirm the deployed address.

screens.title: Public State Variables and Auto-Generated Getters
screens.narratorSegment: Solidity generates getter functions for public state variables automatically. When a variable is declared public, the compiler creates a view function with the variable's name. That means you can call contract. methods. variableName(). call() to fetch the stored value. This shorthand is convenient because you do not need to write a separate getter function in Solidity. Practical example: in SimpleStorage the variables data and owner are declared public. After creating a contract instance in Web3. js, call simpleStorage. methods. data(). call() to get the stored number. Call simpleStorage. methods. owner(). call() to get the owner address saved at construction. Because these getters are view functions, they run locally and cost no gas. Be careful with types. For example, numeric values are returned as strings representing integers. For token balances that follow ERC-20 conventions, values are returned in Wei-like smallest units. Convert them with web3. utils. fromWei or equivalent conversion before displaying to users. A common misconception is that calling the variable directly as a property will return the value. You must call the generated function via contract. methods. The getter pattern keeps your UI code aligned with the contract ABI and prevents accidental transactions.

keyIdea.title: Public variables
keyIdea.text: Public state variables produce view getters accessible with contract.methods.variableName().call(). Convert returned units when needed.

content.html:
Definition › Public State Variables
Automatic getter behavior
Declare a variable public in Solidity and the compiler exposes a view function with the same name.
Example call
simpleStorage.methods.data().call() returns the stored integer as a string.
Type handling
Numeric outputs are strings; token values often require unit conversion with web3.utils.fromWei.
Analogy
Think of public variables as auto-generated read-only endpoints on the contract API. Your UI queries these endpoints without submitting a transaction.
Key Takeaway
Use the generated getters for simple reads and remember to convert units for display.

screens.title: Fetching Past Events with getPastEvents
screens.narratorSegment: Events are the contract's way of emitting structured logs to the blockchain. When a contract emits an event, the data is stored in logs and can be queried later. Web3. js exposes contract. getPastEvents(eventName, options) to retrieve these logs. The returned array contains event objects with returnValues, blockNumber, and transactionHash, which are useful for UIs and analytics. A typical query sets fromBlock and toBlock to limit the search. For performance on public networks, narrow this range. You may also filter by indexed parameters to limit results server-side. For example, DataChanged has an indexed changer field. Using a filter like { filter: { changer: '0x...' } } narrows the results to relevant entries. Concrete example: call simpleStorage. getPastEvents('DataChanged', { fromBlock: 0, toBlock: 'latest' }) to fetch all DataChanged events in a local Ganache instance. Then iterate over events and read event. returnValues. changer, event. returnValues. oldValue, and event. returnValues. newValue. Each event also exposes blockNumber and transactionHash for display. Common pitfalls: querying a huge block range on a public node can be slow and may hit provider rate limits. Always paginate or narrow the block range where possible.

keyIdea.title: Event queries
keyIdea.text: Use getPastEvents with block range and optional filters to efficiently retrieve historical logs and decode returnValues for UI displays.

content.html:
Process Flow › getPastEvents
How to query
Call getPastEvents with the event name and an options object. Read returnValues for emitted data.
const pastEvents = await simpleStorage.getPastEvents('DataChanged', {
  fromBlock: 0,
  toBlock: 'latest'
});

pastEvents.forEach((event) => {
  console.log(event.returnValues.changer, event.returnValues.oldValue, event.returnValues.newValue);
});
Best practices
  • Limit fromBlock/toBlock to avoid heavy queries on public nodes.
  • Use indexed parameters and the filter option to narrow results.
  • Paginate or run range queries if you need large histories.
Example event object
Each event includes returnValues, blockNumber, transactionHash, and event name for easy consumption.

screens.title: .call() vs .send() — A clear contrast
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the difference between. call() and. send() is essential. Use. call() for view and pure functions, which execute locally and cost no gas. Use. send() for functions that change state, because they must be included in a mined transaction and will consume gas. If you call a state-changing function with. call(), it will run locally and return a result, but it will not update the blockchain. That often surprises learners who expect the state to change. Concrete contrast: calling setData(42). call() may return a value indicating what execution would compute, but it does not persist the new data. Calling setData(42). send({ from: account }) will create a transaction, require signing, and update the contract's storage once mined. Common mistake: accidentally using. send() for view functions. That wastes gas and may require user interaction through a signer. Conversely, mistakenly using. call() for an intended state change will leave the application in the same state and create subtle UX bugs. A helpful rule: ask whether the blockchain state must change. If yes, you need a transaction with. send(). If no, use. call(). For UI design, keep reads fast and reserve transactions for explicit user actions. This contrast keeps resources efficient and user flows predictable.

keyIdea.title: Call vs Send
keyIdea.text: .call() reads locally and is gas-free. .send() creates transactions and is required for state changes; do not swap them accidentally.

content.html:
Comparison › .call() vs .send()
.call()
Executes locally on node. No gas. Use for view/pure functions and UI queries.
Example
const v = await contract.methods.getData().call();
.send()
Creates a transaction, costs gas, must be signed. Use for state-changing functions.
Example
await contract.methods.setData(42).send({ from: userAddress });
Key Takeaway

Decide by intent: reads use .call(); state changes require .send(). Mistaking one for the other leads to wasted gas or no state update.

keyIdea.title: ERC-20 read
keyIdea.text: Query token metadata and balances with .call() and convert units for display using web3.utils.fromWei.

content.html:
Terminal Demo › readToken.js
Starter code
const Web3 = require('web3');
const web3 = new Web3('http://127.0.0.1:7545');

const myTokenABI = [ /* ... token ABI ... */ ];
const myTokenAddress = '0x...';

async function queryTokenContract() {
  if (myTokenAddress === '0x...' || myTokenABI.length === 0) {
    console.error('ERROR: Update ABI and address.');
    return;
  }

  const myToken = new web3.eth.Contract(myTokenABI, myTokenAddress);
  const name = await myToken.methods.name().call();
  const symbol = await myToken.methods.symbol().call();
  const totalSupplyWei = await myToken.methods.totalSupply().call();
  const totalSupply = web3.utils.fromWei(totalSupplyWei, 'ether');

  const accounts = await web3.eth.getAccounts();
  const balanceWei = await myToken.methods.balanceOf(accounts[0]).call();
  const balance = web3.utils.fromWei(balanceWei, 'ether');

  console.log('Token:', name, symbol);
  console.log('Total Supply:', totalSupply);
  console.log('Balance:', balance);
}

queryTokenContract();
Console example
Token Name: Cohortia Token (CHT) Total Supply: 1000 CHT Balance of 0xabc...: 1000 CHT
Tip
When converting totalSupply, confirm the token decimals to use the correct unit conversion.

screens.title: Filtering and Performance When Querying Events
screens.narratorSegment: When fetching events on a busy network, naive queries over the entire chain can be slow or trigger provider limits. Plan queries carefully by specifying fromBlock and toBlock ranges that are as small as possible. If your event has indexed parameters, use the filter option to let the node reduce results before transferring them to your client. For example, if DataChanged indexes the changer address, filter by that address to retrieve only relevant events. If you need a long history, paginate your queries by splitting the block range into smaller windows. Request events in sequential batches and aggregate results locally. This reduces memory overhead and avoids timeouts. Also consider caching results in your backend when possible to minimize repeated heavy queries for the same range. A concrete pattern: request events for the last 5,000 blocks when updating a recent activity feed, then periodically fetch older ranges in the background. When debugging, check returned event. blockNumber and transactionHash to verify ordering and to cross-reference with chain explorers or local node logs. Finally, be mindful of provider-specific limits. Public RPC endpoints may throttle large ranges. When developing, prefer a local node like Ganache or an archival node if you need deep history.

keyIdea.title: Event performance
keyIdea.text: Use block range limits, indexed filters, pagination, and caching to make event queries performant and reliable.

content.html:
Process Flow › Event Performance
Practical strategies
  • Narrow your fromBlock and toBlock range.
  • Use indexed event filters to reduce returned results.
  • Paginate large histories into smaller ranges.
  • Cache frequent queries in your backend where appropriate.
Example filter
const events = await myToken.getPastEvents('Transfer', {
  fromBlock: 100,
  toBlock: 200,
  filter: { from: '0xabc...' }
});
Key Takeaway
Be deliberate with blocks and filters. Performance depends on careful query design and provider limits.

screens.title: Integrating Read Operations into a React dApp
screens.narratorSegment: When integrating read operations into a React application, treat contract calls as asynchronous data sources. Create a service that instantiates the contract once and exports functions that perform. call() reads. Components should call these services inside effects and manage loading and error state. For example, fetch token metadata on mount and then fetch balances for the connected account when the account changes. Use clear UX patterns for latency and errors. Show a loading indicator while awaiting. call() results. Display friendly error messages if the node is unreachable or if the ABI/address is invalid. Also convert returned numeric strings to displayable units before rendering. For repeated queries like balances, consider polling on an interval or using block subscriptions if you need near-real-time updates. A misconception to avoid is performing contract instantiation inside every render. Instantiate the contract once and reuse it. Another pitfall is leaking unhandled promises; cancel or ignore outdated requests when components unmount. Finally, for event-driven UIs, fetch recent events with getPastEvents and append new ones as transactions occur, maintaining a consistent activity feed. These patterns keep the UI responsive, predictable, and maintainable while leveraging gas-free reads effectively.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we focus on read operations using Web3. js. Read operations call contract functions that do not change blockchain state. These are typically labeled as view or pure in Solidity and can be executed locally on a connected node. You will learn why these calls cost no gas, how to create a JavaScript contract instance using an ABI and address, and how to call view and pure functions with. call(). We also cover event queries. Smart contracts emit events to log important actions. You will see how to use getPastEvents to retrieve those logs, read their returnValues, and filter by block ranges or indexed fields. That makes building transaction histories and audit UIs straightforward. This chapter emphasizes concrete examples. You will follow a SimpleStorage demo and an ERC-20 token read activity. By the end, you will understand the difference between. call() and. send(), how public variables produce automatic getters, and common mistakes to avoid like using the wrong ABI or an incorrect address. Think about a UI that needs a token balance or a registry lookup — read operations are the efficient, correct tool for that job. Ready to explore contract instantiation, data reads, and historical logs? Let’s begin.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to create a usable Web3. js contract instance, call view and pure functions with. call(), and fetch historical events with getPastEvents. First, you'll learn the exact inputs required to instantiate a contract: a contract ABI and a deployed address. That step is essential because Web3. js relies on the ABI to encode and decode function inputs and outputs. Next, you will practice calling view and pure functions using. call(), understanding its gas-free, local-execution behavior. You will test reading a stored variable and the automatically generated getter for public variables. Then you will learn how to query event logs, interpret returnValues, and limit searches with fromBlock and toBlock. Each objective is practical. You will run a SimpleStorage read demo, then apply the same patterns to an ERC-20 token to query name, symbol, totalSupply, and an account balance. These skills matter because efficient read operations power responsive UIs and analytics without unnecessary transactions.

Each objective pairs with a short verification task. To confirm you can instantiate a contract, grab an ABI and deployed address from a local Ganache deployment and create web3. eth. Contract(ABI, address). You will verify the instance by calling a simple getter like owner() or data(). To practice view and pure calls, run a local script that calls getData(). call() and observes the returned value. For pure functions, pass inputs and confirm the computation matches expectations. For event retrieval, run setData to emit DataChanged events, then use getPastEvents to fetch them and read returnValues. changer and returnValues. newValue. Finally, apply these reads to an ERC-20 contract. Query name(), symbol(), totalSupply(), and balanceOf(account) in a script. Convert token totals from Wei-like units to human decimals with web3. utils. fromWei. Each verification step demonstrates the read semantics and exposes common mistakes like forgetting to replace the placeholder contract address. These short checks help you move from code to reliable UIs quickly.

Read operations are contract calls that do not alter blockchain state. In Solidity these appear as view or pure functions. A view function may read state variables but does not modify them. A pure function does not even read state; it only computes a result using its inputs. Both categories can be executed locally by your connected node, so they do not create transactions and do not consume gas. Why this matters: user interfaces frequently need current values such as balances, ownership, or computed results. Using. call() for view and pure functions makes these queries fast and free. For example, a dApp that displays a token balance calls balanceOf(address). call() to get the value immediately. A pure function that computes a price ratio from input numbers can be called to preview a calculation without writing to the ledger. A common misconception is to think. call() will change state. It will not. If you need to change state you must send a transaction with. send(). Another pitfall is assuming view calls always read the chain exactly the same across nodes; the node's state and syncing status matter. For quick UIs and analytics, view and pure calls are the correct, efficient tool. Key takeaway: use. call() for reads, and reserve. send() for actions that must change the blockchain.

Instantiating a contract in Web3. js is the first practical step for read operations. You need two things: the contract ABI and its deployed address. The ABI is a JSON description of public functions and events. The address tells the node which on-chain bytecode to interact with. With those, create an instance using new web3. eth. Contract(abi, address). That instance exposes a methods object and event helpers. A simple process: 1) Acquire the ABI from the compiled contract artifact. 2) Confirm the deployed address from your deployment tool or Ganache console. 3) In your script, initialize Web3 with a provider and then create the contract instance. 4) Use contract. methods. name(). call() or contract. methods. variable(). call() to fetch data. 5) Use contract. getPastEvents(...) to fetch logs. Concrete example: using the SimpleStorage ABI and a Ganache address, the script creates const simpleStorage = new web3. eth. Contract(simpleStorageABI, simpleStorageAddress). You can then await simpleStorage. methods. getData(). call() to read a number. Watch out for the common mistake of leaving a placeholder address in the code. That will cause errors or null results. Keep ABI and address management consistent between your build and runtime environments to avoid mismatch errors.

In this demo we walk through the SimpleStorage read script. The contract exposes a public data variable and a getData view function. It also emits a DataChanged event when data changes. The script connects to a local Ganache node, creates a web3. eth. Contract with the contract's ABI and deployed address, and then calls getData(). call() and owner(). call(). The. call() method runs the function locally and returns the value without consuming gas. A concrete sequence: first, ensure your simpleStorageAddress is replaced with the correct deployed address. If it still contains a placeholder, the script should bail out and print an error. Next, create the contract instance, then await simpleStorage. methods. getData(). call() to retrieve the current number. Also call simpleStorage. methods. owner(). call() to fetch the owner address created in the constructor. We show console-style output in the code panel. This helps you map code to results. Remember a common mistake is attempting to use. call() to persist a value. setData must be executed as a transaction with. send() if you actually want to change storage. For reads,. call() is the safe and efficient choice. Try this locally and confirm the numbers and addresses match your Ganache deployment.

Solidity generates getter functions for public state variables automatically. When a variable is declared public, the compiler creates a view function with the variable's name. That means you can call contract. methods. variableName(). call() to fetch the stored value. This shorthand is convenient because you do not need to write a separate getter function in Solidity. Practical example: in SimpleStorage the variables data and owner are declared public. After creating a contract instance in Web3. js, call simpleStorage. methods. data(). call() to get the stored number. Call simpleStorage. methods. owner(). call() to get the owner address saved at construction. Because these getters are view functions, they run locally and cost no gas. Be careful with types. For example, numeric values are returned as strings representing integers. For token balances that follow ERC-20 conventions, values are returned in Wei-like smallest units. Convert them with web3. utils. fromWei or equivalent conversion before displaying to users. A common misconception is that calling the variable directly as a property will return the value. You must call the generated function via contract. methods. The getter pattern keeps your UI code aligned with the contract ABI and prevents accidental transactions.

Events are the contract's way of emitting structured logs to the blockchain. When a contract emits an event, the data is stored in logs and can be queried later. Web3. js exposes contract. getPastEvents(eventName, options) to retrieve these logs. The returned array contains event objects with returnValues, blockNumber, and transactionHash, which are useful for UIs and analytics. A typical query sets fromBlock and toBlock to limit the search. For performance on public networks, narrow this range. You may also filter by indexed parameters to limit results server-side. For example, DataChanged has an indexed changer field. Using a filter like { filter: { changer: '0x...' } } narrows the results to relevant entries. Concrete example: call simpleStorage. getPastEvents('DataChanged', { fromBlock: 0, toBlock: 'latest' }) to fetch all DataChanged events in a local Ganache instance. Then iterate over events and read event. returnValues. changer, event. returnValues. oldValue, and event. returnValues. newValue. Each event also exposes blockNumber and transactionHash for display. Common pitfalls: querying a huge block range on a public node can be slow and may hit provider rate limits. Always paginate or narrow the block range where possible.

Understanding the difference between. call() and. send() is essential. Use. call() for view and pure functions, which execute locally and cost no gas. Use. send() for functions that change state, because they must be included in a mined transaction and will consume gas. If you call a state-changing function with. call(), it will run locally and return a result, but it will not update the blockchain. That often surprises learners who expect the state to change. Concrete contrast: calling setData(42). call() may return a value indicating what execution would compute, but it does not persist the new data. Calling setData(42). send({ from: account }) will create a transaction, require signing, and update the contract's storage once mined. Common mistake: accidentally using. send() for view functions. That wastes gas and may require user interaction through a signer. Conversely, mistakenly using. call() for an intended state change will leave the application in the same state and create subtle UX bugs. A helpful rule: ask whether the blockchain state must change. If yes, you need a transaction with. send(). If no, use. call(). For UI design, keep reads fast and reserve transactions for explicit user actions. This contrast keeps resources efficient and user flows predictable.
